title: Angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2)
hookLine: welcome strangers; some have hosted angels without knowing

lines: THE HOTTEST PART OF THE DAY.
cards: It's the hottest part of the day. An old man sits in the doorway of his tent. He looks up, and three strangers are standing nearby.
He doesn't wait for them to ask. He runs, in that heat. He bows and begs them to stay.
He fetches water to wash their feet, tells his wife to bake bread from the good flour, picks out a calf himself. He calls it a little bread. It's a feast.

He stands under a tree while they eat. It's Abraham, in Genesis eighteen, and before the day is over he learns who his guests really were. Much later, a letter in the New Testament seems to remember that afternoon.

teach.b: Hospitality. The New Testament's Greek word is philoxenia: philo, love; xenos, stranger. Love of the stranger.
Not of your friends, which is easy, but of the person you don't know yet. Near its end, the letter to the Hebrews puts it on a short list of how to live.
In the King James Bible: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Unawares: without knowing.

Readers have long heard Abraham in that line, though the letter never names him. The visitors at his tent turn out to be messengers of God, and in the story one of them promises that old Sarah will have a son.
Abraham didn't welcome them because they were angels. He welcomed them, and they turned out to be. In the world of these stories, this was no small courtesy.
A traveler far from home depended on someone's open door for food and safety. Opening it could be a lifeline, and it could cost you.
In Matthew, Jesus says the king will say at the end: "I was a stranger, and ye took me in."
Saint Benedict, writing a rule for monks, said every guest should be welcomed as Christ, quoting that same line.

teach.h: I WAS A STRANGER, AND YE TOOK ME IN.
teach.b: Jewish tradition treasures the story too: welcoming guests is counted a mitzvah, a commandment, and Abraham's open tent is its picture.
The idea is simple, and harder than it sounds: the person at your door might carry more than you can see.

how: Many Christians practice hospitality by welcoming visitors at church, opening their homes for meals, and hosting travelers; some monasteries keep guesthouses for visitors, following Saint Benedict's rule to receive guests as Christ.

o: welcoming strangers, people you don't know yet
a fee travelers pay for a night at an inn

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Abraham welcomed the visitors because he knew they were angels
he welcomed them first. who they were came out later.
the Greek word for hospitality means love of strangers
philoxenia: philo, love, and xenos, stranger.
the letter to the Hebrews names Abraham in this line
it says only that some have entertained angels unawares. readers hear Abraham in it.

games.q: you're Abraham, resting in the heat at your tent door. three strangers appear nearby. what do you do?
o: stay in the shade and wait to see what they want.
run to them, bow, and beg them to stay and eat.
send a servant to ask who they are.
games.why: he runs, in the heat of the day, and serves them a feast he calls a little bread. only later does he learn who his guests were.

practice: Picture your own door, at home or at work, and the people who come to it that you barely notice: the delivery driver, the new person on the team, the neighbor you've nodded at for two years.

Pick one face and imagine offering them something small to drink, water, a coffee, a cold soda. If you pray, ask to see that person clearly; if you don't, simply hold their face a moment with a little more warmth than usual.
